Where to read more
Adams, Khan, Raeside and White on the research cycle, and on the literature review and critical reading. That DOI resolves to the 2007 edition, titled Research Methods for Graduate Business and Social Science Students, so check the chapter numbers against whichever copy you open.
Sarasvathy on effectuation is the theory paper behind “start from your means”. Read it for the list of resources it implies, not for a law about entrepreneurs.
Arrow, Economic welfare and the allocation of resources for invention is where public value comes from. Knowledge is expensive to make and cheap to copy, so whoever makes it cannot charge the people who benefit.
McLean and Pontiff is the private-value paper, and it is the most useful twenty pages in this list if your interest is finance.
Sandberg and Alvesson separate looking for a hole in the literature, which they call gap-spotting, from challenging what the literature takes for granted, which they call problematization. It is a distinction for people writing for journals rather than for this course, so read it only if you want the research-side version of today.

title: 3 · Finding the question
text:
What makes a good idea

You need a way to quickly evaluate ideas, otherwise you hang on to less interesting ideas for too long.
An good idea has to check a few boxes:


Importance. Somebody is better off knowing the answer.
Feasible. One can actually get the answer with existing data and methods.
Novelty. The answer is not already known.
Fit. The idea is great for your team. You have the skills and comparative advantage to tackle it.


You can rank ideas based on these criteria to pick ideas with high potential for your team.


One and a half minutes. Put the four up and do not explain them yet. One slide each follows.
Say why this comes first. You already have ideas, so the useful thing is not another way to generate them. It is a way to sort them fast. The cost of having no test is not that you pick a bad idea on purpose. It is that you stay with a mediocre one for weeks because nothing told you to drop it.
Say that the four are not weighted equally in this course. Feasible is the one that kills projects in March, so it gets the whole second half of the hour.
Say also that they pull against each other. The most important questions are usually the least feasible, and the most feasible are usually the least new. A project is a choice about where to sit between them, not a search for a question that scores full marks on all four.
The fourth is the one they will not expect and it is the one that stops a team adopting somebody else’s good idea. Flag it here and let the fourth slide do the work.

title: 3 · Finding the question
text:
What makes a question important

Answering the question provide value to someone.
The value you bring can be a private or a public good.
Private good: e.g. you shed light on an untapped market segment for a company (value is derived by acting upon the private information, not publishing it)
Public good: e.g. you shed light on how changing a policy could improve economic surplus (value is derived by publishing)
In academia, the important is often measure by how many other academics find the work useful (determines journals and drives citations)
Key idea: someone is better off after we responded to this question.


Ninety seconds. This is the test that the last two cohorts failed, and it is the one the room will resist, because a big topic feels important.
Push on the difference. Climate change is large. Whether a flood changes what a lender charges is important, because somebody acts on the answer.
Do not resolve who acts and who pays here. That is the next block, and it is where this test gets its second half.

title: 3 · Finding the question
text:
What makes an answer valuable


Somebody or some organization has a decision to make that would benefit from it, or a whole agenda cannot move without it.
If you cannot identify the people or organizations benefiting from the new knowledge, then it’s unclear this is important.
Public good value is shared: many people are better off and you cannot stop anyone using the answer, so it is hard to charge for and it gets published.
Private good value can be kept: one person’s decision changes, and that person can keep the answer to themselves, so somebody pays for it.
Both are fine for this project. Private value has greater traction in private industry.



Two and a half minutes. This is the fourth filter, would anybody act differently, arriving early. Say the word value and leave the slide up.
The bullet that says the test is whether the answer can be kept is what makes quiz item 1 work, because a student who learned “private means somebody acts” picks the wrong distractor without it.
Neither definition uses the word excludable. Say “you cannot stop anyone using it” out loud too, because the term is not what is being examined.
The theory behind the public half is Arrow 1962 on knowledge as a non-excludable good, cited on the companion page and not on the slide.
Say plainly that the grade does not prefer private.

title: 3 · Finding the question
section: Who acts on the answer or pays for it
text:
Who acts on the answer or pays for it

1 · attention and stock prices · private value An investment fund would pay for this while it is the only one holding the answer. Ask instead whether small investors lose money and your reader is a regulator, which is a different project.


2 · extreme weather and damage · both Finance ministries and the World Bank act on a published number. Insurers would pay for the same number, because it is what they price the cover on.


One minute. The lesson is the sentence under each label, the one that names who acts or pays. A team that can fill it has passed filter 4. Read both of those sentences out; the labels can be said in one word each.
Each block names its item in three or four words, because the vote slide is gone by now and “1 · private” on its own tells a student nothing.
Insurers on the screen is reinsurers in fact. Say reinsurers if you want, after the plain word, and do not spend a sentence on the difference.
The plan draws this reveal as a three-column table. It is set as two stacked rows instead, because the first “why” cell is twenty-four words and a cell that long does not fit at this root size.
Item 1 is Team D’s sentence shown as a buyer it has, not as a verdict. The verdict on signal-on-returns sits on “Private value is easier to sell, and it evaporates when published”, one slide from here.
Gate. This slide is on screen by 2:24. If it is not, read it as one item only, and drop “Private value is easier to sell, and it evaporates when published” to its first and last bullet. That saves a minute and a half.


Two minutes. Start the count-down at thirty, projected beside the slide, and say nothing until it ends. It shows this write’s own seconds and it is the only thing that ends the write. Write, do not talk. Nobody reads one out.
This line is the pitch’s why-it-matters line, written while the examples are on the screen. It goes on the question sheet, the slate on the printing list, this afternoon in the same words, which is why the last bullet exists: the strip is a personal half sheet that is never collected, and it is the thing most likely to be left on a chair at 3:15. The same instruction is printed at the top of the slate sheet, which the sheet itself calls the question sheet.
Transition line: value says why, and the shape says what you can claim.

title: 3 · Finding the question
text:
What makes a question feasible

You can get the data, in the time you have, with the skills on the team.
Feasibility is about resources. It is not about whether the question could be answered by somebody.
Most projects fail here, so it is critical to evaluate this as early as possible.
A check: can you pin point the data you are using (if using secondary data) or have an idea of the platform to run your experiments (if working with primary data).


Ninety seconds. Say plainly that this is the one that does the killing, and that it is why the second half of the hour is one long exercise in it.
Checked, not assumed, is the phrase to repeat. It comes back on the map as the difference between a have and a need.
The whole resource map is this test taken seriously, so this slide is its promise. Do not open the map here.

title: 3 · Finding the question
text:
What makes a question novel

Nobody has already answered it, and you know that because you went and looked.
Requires that you read and look around extensively.
New does not mean nobody has worked on the topic (that could be a sign this is not important). Instead, it means this answer is not already out there (e.g. a publication, a product or service line, etc.).
A marginal change to published work is new, but not as important (you need to recognize this).
The check: what is the closest study to ours, and clearly identify how your study sheds light on something the previous study did not provide any insight.


Ninety seconds. This is the test that sends them to the literature, and it is the only reason this course asks them to read.
Tie it back to the second route without naming a team. A marginal change passes this test at the low end, and that is acceptable for one semester as long as the team knows where it is sitting.
The honest failure here is not being unoriginal. It is not having looked.

title: 3 · Finding the question
section: Private value disappears once it is published
text:
Private value disappears once it is published


McLean and Pontiff collected 97 published rules for picking stocks that beat the market.
On average a rule earned 26 percent less on later data than in the study that found it, and 58 percent less once it was in print.
A rule is worth money while one trading desk is the only one using it, and about half that once it is in a journal.
A search-traffic signal regressed on next-day returns has no trading desk and no journal, so it has neither kind of value.
If an answer is worth money and nobody has produced it, ask why, and read to check that nobody has.
A public good does not lose its value like this.


McLean and Pontiff (2016), Does Academic Research Destroy Stock Return Predictability?, Journal of Finance 71(1), 5 to 32

Ninety seconds. This is why signal-on-returns is a fine desk memo and a bad capstone.
Nobody in the room has to have read a finance paper. Return predictor is “a rule for picking stocks that beat the market”, out of sample is “on later data”, and both are said that way on the slide.
The figures and the DOI are verified, so they go on the slide as numbers and not as “about”. Do not say “near zero”: it was wrong and contradicted the paper cited one bullet above it.
The last bullet is meeting 1’s line on what reading is for, turned into a reason to go to the literature.

title: 3 · Finding the question
section: What makes a question a good fit for you
text:
What makes a question a good fit for you

A question can be important, feasible and new, and still not be a good fit.
Fit is two things: the skills your team actually has, and whether you care about it.
A question nobody on the team can execute is somebody else’s project, however good it is.
The check: do we know the skills we have in the team? Do we have the excitement and commitment for this? Are we well organized and know who does what?


Ninety seconds. This is the instructor’s own fourth test and it is the one that is missing from every version of this advice they will read elsewhere.
Say the failure case plainly. A team adopts a question because it sounds important, nobody on it can do the hardest part, and by February the project is being done badly by the one person who can.
Interest is not softness. The question that gets finished is the one somebody still wants to answer when it has stopped being fun, and that is a feasibility fact rather than a preference.
This is also the argument for the inventory on “Start from what you have”, forty minutes from now. Do not open it here, just plant it.

title: 3 · Finding the question
section: A project can take different shapes
text:
A project can take different shapes










The question it asks
For example




1 Evaluation
Did it work? Somebody changed something and you measure what it did
Did the loyalty card raise what people spend?


2 Preference and pricing
What would people choose and pay? Nobody has decided yet, so you ask them
Would shoppers pay more for a lower carbon label?


3 Prediction and risk
What happens next? You need the number, not the reason
Which customers will cancel next quarter?


4 Diagnosis
Why is this so uneven? Something varies and nobody knows why
Why do some stores sell twice what similar stores do?


5 Feasibility
Is this opportunity real, and what is in the way?
Is there a market for this product in Kenya?


6 Measurement
How much of this is there? Nobody has counted it, so you build the number
What does one flood actually cost a county?


7 Valuation
What is this worth? You price it against things that already carry prices
What is a water view worth on a house?





The same interest can usually be turned into three of these, so pick the one you can answer.


Three and a half minutes. This slide defines the five. The next one kills them, so do not give away the failures here.
Read the middle column out. It is written for somebody who has never taken an econometrics course, and the examples are there so nobody has to guess what the label means.
Rows six and seven were added on 2026-09-09 because five did not cover the room. Measurement is how much of this is there when nobody has counted it, and it is where the climate damage question sits. Valuation is what is this worth, priced against comparable things, and it is where the asset pricing question sits. Neither team is named on the screen.
The old version of this slide showed only the failure column, which named five categories it never defined. It was cryptic and it was cut on 2026-09-09.
The can-claim column is spoken rather than shown, and all four columns are printed on the companion page. Say the one line that matters: one and two can support a claim about cause, three cannot and must not pretend to, four is a description that points at a cause somebody could test later, and five needs at least one piece of the team’s own evidence or it is a literature review.
Then say Team H’s sentence as three shapes, as a gift. The sentence is “does AI advice move a non-expert closer to a good decision, or just swap their overconfidence for the model’s?”. Evaluation: did people given AI advice decide better than people without it? Preference: which advice format do people choose, and what would they pay for it? Prediction: who over-relies, and can you tell in advance?
A team that hears its own interest in one of those three has found its afternoon’s first job.

title: 3 · Finding the question
text:
Ideas arrive in three ways

From the world. Something you noticed, or a decision somebody has to make.
From previous work. A marginal change to something already published.
From data. A file you can already reach, worked backwards to a question.


One slide each follows, and each one ends with the thing that route leaves missing.


One minute. Put the three up and take them one at a time afterwards.
Say the shape of the block before it starts: the world lacks data, previous work lacks novelty, data lacks a decision. They will hear each of those again on its own slide, so do not explain them here.
Meeting 1’s page calls the data route “route 5”. Say once, and only once, that the five collapsed into three, because a gap and an extension are both previous work, and an anomaly and a decision are both the world.

title: 3 · Finding the question
text:
Getting ideas from the world

From the world: a problem you saw, and it usually arrives without being sought.
It comes from the news, from a conversation with a colleague, or from a job you have done yourself.
The good ones often come out of an unexpected conversation rather than out of sitting down to think.
You start with the problem and go looking for data afterwards, so data is the row most likely to be empty.


Ninety seconds. This is the route most of the room arrived on.
No team is named on this slide or on the two that follow. Naming one makes the route a verdict on their question, and the three routes are not a ranking.
Say once, and only once, that meeting 1’s page calls the data route “route 5”, and that the five collapsed into three, because a gap and an extension are both previous work, and an anomaly and a decision are both the world.
Gate. This slide is on screen by 2:11. If it is not, run all three route slides at a minute each by dropping the third bullet from every one.

title: 3 · Finding the question
text:
Getting ideas from previous work

From previous work: you take an existing idea, generally published, and change it at the margin.
The change is usually a new setting, a new period, or a limitation the original authors name themselves.
Read the limitations section, because that is where the authors write down what they could not do.
This route tends to be marginal, and saying so is honest rather than modest. For one semester it is the right size.


Ninety seconds. Marginal is the instructor’s own word for this route and it is not a criticism. Say it plainly.
The data usually exists already, because the first study needed it. What is missing here is novelty, and novelty is not a row on the map, which is why the reading has to happen before the data work rather than after it.
Do not say which team in this room is on this route. Several are.

title: 3 · Finding the question
text:
Getting ideas from data

From data: you start from a file you can reach and work backwards to a question it could answer.
Data is usually the binding constraint, so this route makes the constraint visible on day one.
Expect to go back and forth. You get the file, find what it does not contain, and revise the question.
That revising is not the plan failing. It is the loop the rest of this hour is about.


Ninety seconds. This is the instructor’s own account of the route: the data constrains the question, and the question moves.
Gloss Dewey here, in one clause, because it is named on the access ladder forty minutes from now and nowhere in between: the data marketplace the business school subscribes to, free to them, and approval takes days.
The reverse-engineering is the next slide, so do not deliver the warning here. The fourth bullet is its set-up, and it is also the first statement of the loop the resource map draws.

title: 3 · Finding the question
text:
Working backwards from data honestly

What could this data answer?
Which of those would anybody act on?
What does it not contain that you would need?
You are allowed to walk away from the data.
Starting from data is the only route where the data is already in hand, so nothing looks missing, and only the question of who would act can kill it.


Ninety seconds. The first four lines are meeting 1’s, said once and not re-taught.
The fifth is the new thing and it is why the slide survives. It is the hook into “What your question needs against what you have”, and it is the tell the shared case turns on after the break.
The map words belong to that slide and not to this one, so do not say “the data row is full and the gap column is empty” here. Say what the bullet says.
If the 2:16 gate is missed, the whole slide becomes one spoken sentence on “Which route did your team’s question come from?” and the fifth line is the sentence.

title: 8 · Research designs I
text:
Session A · 2:00–3:15
Three designs, each drawn before it is described. Experiments first. Randomisation cuts every arrow into treatment, so there is no back door left to close. Then the decisions that actually make one work. What is the unit you randomise — the person, the store, the week? How many arms can you afford before each one is too thin? Why you check balance afterwards, and what a failure would mean. And pre-registration, the cheapest honesty device in research: say what you will test before you look, and specification search stops being available to you. Instrumental variables next. An arrow into treatment, and none into the outcome except through it. The exclusion restriction is that missing arrow, which is why it cannot be tested. Then regression discontinuity: nothing else jumps at the cutoff. For each, what variation it exploits, what it assumes, how it fails, and what it looks like done well.

title: 12 · Speaking
text:
Session A · 2:00–3:15
Same skeleton, new medium. Your talk is the outline from meeting 10 with pictures on it, and the pictures are the ones you rebuilt in meeting 11. Then the rule that does most of the work: one claim per slide, and the claim is the slide title. “Methodology” is a label. “We compare stores on either side of a state border, so the weather and the season are the same on both sides” is a claim. “Results” is a label. “Basket size rose 4% in relaunch stores and did not move next door” is a claim. Read your titles alone, top to bottom, with nothing else on the screen. You should have the argument. If you do not, the deck does not contain one, and no amount of delivery will put it there. Next, the thing everybody does and nobody defends. No bullet lists. A bullet list is an outline you stopped converting into sentences. The room reads it faster than you can say it, so you lose them for the rest of the slide, and you end up reading your own slide out loud to people who finished it. Then the two thirty-seconds. The first thirty seconds say what the question is and why anybody should care. Not your name. Not an agenda slide. Not thanking anyone. The last thirty seconds say what you want: in this genre, what will exist by May and what you need to get there. Everything in between is negotiable; those two are not. Then structure by length, because they are different objects. Five minutes is five slides — the question, the decision somebody makes differently, the design and the assumption carrying it, the data and how you actually get it, and what exists by May. Fifteen minutes is that same spine with room for the graph, one alternative explanation you considered and rejected, and the limitation stated plainly. It is not five minutes with more slides on the end. Then questions, which is where most pitches are actually won or lost. Three kinds arrive. Clarification: answer it in one sentence and move. Challenge: answer first, then explain, and do not relitigate the whole talk. And the one you cannot answer, which is the one worth practising. The answer is “I don’t know,” followed by what would settle it. That sentence costs you nothing and a bluff costs you the room, because the people asking do this for a living and they can hear it. Know your numbers cold — sample size, the headline magnitude, where the data comes from, what it costs — because those are what get asked, and fumbling them undoes twenty good minutes. Then delivery, briefly, and this is not charm school. You will talk too fast, so rehearse standing up and out loud, once, with a clock; reading it in your head is not rehearsal and it is why teams over-run. Pause after a claim. Silence is what makes it land, and it is the only tool here that works on everybody. Stand where the room can see you, not behind the laptop and not in the projector beam, and never turn your back to read your own slide. And plan for the deck failing, because eventually it does. Know your first three claims by heart. Carry a PDF you can open from a phone. Be able to give the whole thing with no slides at all, which if the titles are claims you nearly can. Finally, the genre you actually face. You are pitching a research plan to people who will never read the paper. They are not checking your work. They are deciding whether to fund it, staff it, or wait. So they ask three things: so what would you do differently, how confident are you, and what does it cost. A talk built for a seminar answers none of them. I will give you the same two-minute pitch twice at the front — once with an agenda slide and bullet lists, once with claim titles and nothing else — and you will tell me which one you can repeat back.

title: 12 · Speaking
text:
Session B · 3:30–4:30
Every session B opens with a ten-minute team check-in: what you did since last week, what is stuck, and who is doing what next. Written down, and handed in with that session’s work.
Ten minutes of team check-in first, with one agenda item today: who says which slide at meeting 14, and who holds the clock. Then the shared case. I give a five-minute pitch from the front and it is deliberately bad — an agenda slide, a title called “Results,” four bullets a slide, the claim arriving on slide 4, forty seconds over, and one question answered with a bluff. Everybody scores the same pitch on the same card. What did the first thirty seconds do? Where did the claim first appear? What was the ask? Then the part that gets compared: every team rewrites my five slide titles as claims, working from the same five labels, and the best set goes on the screen next to mine. Same object, same constraint, so a good rewrite and a lazy one are visible side by side. Then the dress rehearsal, which is the rest of the hour. Order is drawn at random. Every team pitches its own project, three minutes, hard stop, five slides with claim titles. Then the room attacks — and it attacks the argument, not the delivery. Attacks come in four named types and nothing else counts: the data cannot answer this question, the assumption carrying the estimate is false in this setting, the comparison group is not comparable, or the answer would not change anyone’s decision. “You seemed nervous” is not an attack and scores nothing. Points for attacks that land, as always. Each team leaves with four things in writing. Their actual clock time. The attack slips, each naming its type. One line from me. And the one that does the real work: before any discussion, two other teams write down in a single sentence the claim they think you just made, and you write down the claim you meant. You leave holding both. Where those two sentences differ is your meeting-14 rewrite, and you have three weeks to close the gap. Handed in before you leave: the five-slide dress-rehearsal deck, your written thirty-second opening and thirty-second close, and the claim-we-meant against claim-they-heard sheet.

title: 7 · Model failures
text:
Session A · 2:00–3:15
Two families of failure, and they are not the same problem. Bias moves the number. False precision leaves the number where it is and shrinks the error bar around it. Bias first, and there are four. Selection and sorting: the retention email went to the customers already most likely to renew, so the lift is who was picked, not what was sent. Omitted variables, with a rule for the direction — the omitted thing’s effect on the outcome, times its correlation with the treatment. Two signs multiplied. You can usually work out which way you are wrong before you have the data. Measurement error next. Classical error in the variable you care about pulls the estimate toward zero, always: self-reported spend, survey income, recalled hours. Non-classical error does not. People round, they under-report, and top-coded income errs one way only. Then it can go anywhere. Fourth, endogeneity and reverse causality. More police, more crime. The firm raised price in the quarter demand was strongest. And then the question I will ask of every one of them: does more data fix it? No. A biased estimate with a million rows is a more precisely wrong number. Then the quieter family, which leaves the estimate untouched. Dependence ignored: five hundred shoppers in ten stores is closer to ten observations than five hundred, and Bertrand, Duflo and Mullainathan found placebo policies in state panels rejecting at 45% instead of 5%. Multiple testing: twenty subgroups, one significant, one slide. Specification search: Silberzahn gave 29 teams one dataset and one question, and got estimates from 0.89 to 2.93. None of the three moves the number. All three make you sure of it. Last, the fixes and their ceiling. Conditioning on observables, drawn on the graph — which back doors a set of controls closes, and the two controls that make things worse. One sits on the path from cause to effect. One opens a path by being conditioned on. Then matching, which is the same claim made by comparison rather than by regression, and it needs somebody to compare to. If no untreated store looks like your treated stores, there is nothing there. Then the ceiling. LaLonde put observational estimates with controls up against a randomised benchmark, and they did not reproduce it. ‘I added controls’ is a claim about the graph, not a technique. So state the claim out loud, and report how far your coefficient moved when the controls went in.

title: 7 · Model failures
text:
Session B · 3:30–4:30
Every session B opens with a ten-minute team check-in: what you did since last week, what is stuck, and who is doing what next. Written down, and handed in with that session’s work.
Ten minutes of team check-in, then the results-critique cards again — the same eight analysts, dealt fresh, and this time each one has come back with a fix. They added controls. Fifteen minutes to rule on it. Name the failure in the morning’s vocabulary. Say which way it pushes the estimate. Say whether more data would fix it. Then rule on the fix itself: does the control close a back door, sit on the path from cause to effect, or open a door by being conditioned on? Then one team is drawn at random to defend at the front while the room attacks, and we draw again as far as the clock allows. Nobody knows in advance whether they are up. Points for attacks that land, and you have to name what is wrong, not just dislike it. Card 7 is the one to watch. title: 2 · Project teams
text:
The four criteria
Teams were built from what you wrote in the research interest survey, on four criteria.

A similar question. Not the same one. Close enough that you are arguing about the same thing.
Some analysis experience on every team. Somebody has run one before.
Some shared programming language, so you can hand each other code.
Somebody likely to be self-driven, who will push it along.

These four pull against each other, and no set of nine teams satisfies all of them at once. Where they conflicted, the question came first.

Say the method out loud: they wrote it, I read all 41, a language model also read them and proposed groupings of the questions rather than of the people, and I decided. Nothing used name, country, degree or grades.

text:
If you think you are on the wrong team
You do not get to choose your group.

Email me by Friday with a reason, in writing, about the work.
The reason has to be about the question or the skills. Your question is genuinely the one another team is asking. Or you are the third person on your team who can do the same thing, and another team has none.
I have to agree, and a swap has to work both ways. Teams are four and five, so moving you moves somebody else.

Not a reason: my friend is on another team.

You will work with people you did not pick for the rest of your career, and the teams that struggle are almost never the ones that were badly matched.

title: Working in a team
text:
In 2026, GMAC asked 1,100 corporate recruiters what they value in business graduates. They ranked communication first, and problem-solving second. I therefore put more emphasis on those dimensions in your grade.
The same survey asked where graduates fall short. Fewer than half arrive well-prepared on grit, emotional intelligence, or managing people. All three are team skills.
So this page is not a nicety. It is a short toolkit, with sources, for the part of the course that most often goes wrong. The survey is here.

title: Working in a team
section: The four things that actually go wrong
text:
The four things that actually go wrong
The same four, in every capstone course.

Nobody wrote down who does what. So the conscientious person does it all. By October they resent it.
A deadline slips and nothing happens. No consequence was agreed. Nobody wants to be the one who raises it.
The team never says the hard thing. The question is vague, or the data will not arrive. Saying so is uncomfortable, so nobody does.
Everyone finds out in November that the work was split unevenly. By then it cannot be fixed.

Everything below is aimed at one of those four.

title: Working in a team
text:
Tools worth using

The ground rules, and RACI
You write ground rules in meeting 2. Teams usually skip the split of work.
The standard tool is a RACI matrix. For each task, name who is Responsible (does it), Accountable (owns whether it happened), Consulted, and Informed. Accountable is always one person.
It sounds bureaucratic for a team of five. It takes fifteen minutes. It prevents failures 1 and 4, because every deliverable has a name against it.


The weekly check-in
Ten minutes at the start of every session B: what you did, what is stuck, who does what next. In writing, handed in.
This is a stand-up, borrowed from agile practice, and its purpose here is not ceremony — it is that the written record makes an uneven split visible in week 4 rather than week 13. See Derby & Larsen, Agile Retrospectives (2006), for the family of practices it belongs to.


The decision log
One shared document. Every time the team decides something — the question, the outcome variable, the data source — one line: what was decided, when, and why.
Costs nothing, and it is the single best defence against the November conversation that begins “I thought we agreed…”. It also becomes the spine of your work plan, because a decision log read backwards is a methods section.


Psychological safety
This is the best-evidenced finding in the whole area. Teams perform better when members believe they can be wrong out loud. Admitting you are lost has to be safe, or people stop admitting it. That is psychological safety, from Amy Edmondson’s work — “Psychological Safety and Learning Behavior in Work Teams”, Administrative Science Quarterly (1999), and her book The Fearless Organization (2018). Google’s internal Project Aristotle study found it the strongest predictor of team effectiveness among the factors it examined.
The practical version is one sentence. The person who says “I don’t understand what we’re doing” is doing the team a favour. Say that out loud in meeting 2. Then behave as if it is true.


Conflict, when it comes
Fisher & Ury, Getting to Yes (1981), is the standard reference, and its central move is the useful one here: argue about interests, not positions. “I want to use this dataset” is a position. “I want us to finish on time and I don’t trust the other source to arrive” is an interest, and interests can be traded.
Your ground rules should already say when a disagreement comes to me. Use it earlier than feels comfortable.

title: Working in a team
section: What we will use to assess it
text:
What we will use to assess it
Peer evaluation runs twice, at meetings 6 and 12, on CATME — the Comprehensive Assessment of Team Member Effectiveness, developed at Purdue and used by around 17,000 instructors at 2,200 institutions. It scores five dimensions that research has found matter: contributing to the team’s work, interacting with teammates, keeping the team on track, expecting quality, and having the relevant knowledge and skills.
See Loughry, Ohland & Moore, “Development of a Theory-Based Assessment of Team Member Effectiveness”, Educational and Psychological Measurement (2007), and Ohland et al., “The Comprehensive Assessment of Team Member Effectiveness”, Academy of Management Learning & Education (2012). The tool itself is at info.catme.org.
Two things follow. Your rating of your teammates is not a formality — it adjusts individual grades on team work. And the five dimensions are published, so you know in advance what you are being rated on. Read them in week 1 and behave accordingly.

title: Working in a team
section: Frameworks you will hear about — and what they are worth
text:
Frameworks you will hear about — and what they are worth
Business school will hand you several of these. They are not equally supported, and knowing which is which is itself part of the course.



Framework
What it says
What it is worth




Psychological safety (Edmondson)
Teams do better when it is safe to be wrong out loud
Strong. Extensively replicated, and the mechanism is clear


CATME dimensions (Ohland et al.)
Five measurable facets of member effectiveness
Strong. Validated instrument, large samples


Conditions for team effectiveness (Haas & Mortensen, HBR 2016)
Compelling direction, strong structure, supportive context, shared mindset
Good. Practitioner synthesis of a real literature


Tuckman’s stages — forming, storming, norming, performing (1965)
Teams pass through predictable phases
Useful vocabulary, weak evidence. Teams do not reliably move in that order. Use it to name what is happening, not to predict


Belbin team roles (1981)
Nine roles; balance them
Popular, poorly supported. The psychometrics have not held up well. Treat as a conversation starter, not a diagnosis



That last row is worth pausing on. A framework being widely used in business is not evidence that it works — which is the same lesson as the rest of this course, applied to management rather than to data.

title: Permissions and ethics
text:
Two gates stand between your design and your data. They are different kinds of thing.
The IRB is an ethics review. It governs research involving people.
A data-use agreement is a contract. It governs somebody else’s proprietary data.
Both take longer than teams expect. Both have to start in the autumn. Neither is something you can grant yourself.

text:
Does this apply to us?
The IRB governs research with human participants. Two questions decide it:

Is it research? A systematic investigation designed to produce generalisable knowledge. A capstone intended to inform one firm’s decision may not be; one written to say something about people in general is.
Are there human participants? Either you interact with living people — surveys, interviews, experiments, focus groups — or you use identifiable private information about them.

Teams miss the second half. Scraped social media posts count if individuals are identifiable. So do purchased consumer records and administrative microdata.
Cornell’s IRB office publishes the decision tree its own staff use, and it has a branch for class projects. A project whose sole intent is to meet a course requirement, with no intention to use the results for anything else, is not human participant research. A project whose results leave the course, for a publication, a presentation, a thesis or a sponsor’s decision, is. A capstone is the second kind. The tree has a second page for existing data, and the question it asks is whether you can link a row to a living person, directly or through a code, not what the vendor calls the file.
Foot-traffic and card-spend data of the kind on Dewey arrive aggregated and de-identified. That is normally what puts them outside the definition. But you do not get to make that call yourself. When in doubt, ask, and ask early.






You are not the one who decides you are exempt. Even exempt research needs a determination from the IRB. “We decided it was exempt” is not a category.

title: Permissions and ethics
text:
How it works at Cornell
The IRB is administered by Cornell Research Services, East Hill Office Building.
Submissions go through RASS-IRB — rass.cornell.edu/irb, with step-by-step guidance at guide.rass.cornell.edu.
Training comes first. Every person listed on a protocol must complete CITI Program human-participants training. That includes exempt protocols, a requirement since October 2022. It lasts five years.
The IRB issues nothing until every listed person has finished. One teammate who skipped the modules holds up the whole team.
The CITI modules are required of every member of a team whose project involves human participants, and session B of meeting 4 is where each team decides whether that is you. Register at citiprogram.org under the Cornell affiliation, take the course Cornell accepts (it is called IRB Training or IRB Basic), and upload the completion certificate to Canvas before meeting 6, Wednesday September 30. Not there by then costs five participation points. The modules take two to four hours. If your project has no human participants you owe nothing now; if the plan changes later, do the modules that week, before the protocol is drafted. The credential lasts five years and is worth having for the research most of you will run inside a firm.
Three levels of review:








Level
Roughly
What it covers




Exempt
Most classroom surveys of adults on non-sensitive topics
Still requires an IRB determination


Expedited
Minimal-risk research not fitting an exempt category
Reviewed by a member, not the full board


Full board
More than minimal risk, or vulnerable populations
Meets on a schedule — plan around it



Cornell’s own clock, from the IRB office’s page on the life cycle of a protocol: an exemption takes three to four weeks from start to finish, expedited review four to six, and the full board four to eight. The board meets on the first Friday of every month, so its clock is a calendar, not a queue. All three assume a complete submission; an incomplete one goes back and the clock restarts.
Cornell’s own guidance for studies enrolling students asks for submission at least four weeks before enrolment begins, and warns that anything needing an ancillary review takes longer.

title: Permissions and ethics
section: What a protocol actually asks for
text:
What a protocol actually asks for
Less than students fear, but all of it in writing:

What you will do, step by step, from recruitment to analysis
Who your participants are, how many, and how you find them
The instrument itself — the actual survey, the actual script
Consent language — what you tell people before they agree
Risks and benefits, stated honestly. For most survey work the risk is boredom and a small privacy exposure; say so rather than claiming zero
Data handling — where it lives, who sees it, whether it is identifiable, when it is destroyed
A faculty member, since students generally cannot serve as principal investigator on their own. That is me. I am the faculty advisor on your protocol, so the draft goes past me before it goes to the IRB

Writing the instrument early is not bureaucracy tax. It forces you to decide what you are actually measuring, which is meeting 4.

title: Permissions and ethics
text:
Data-use agreements
The second gate, and a different animal. A DUA is a contract, not an ethics review, and it is signed by the university rather than by you — which is why you cannot simply accept a firm’s terms on your team’s behalf, however reasonable they look. If a firm gives you proprietary data, expect legal review on both sides, expect it to take months, and expect restrictions on what you may publish.
At Cornell the Office of Sponsored Programs is the party that enters into agreements for the use of data. Write to osp_dua@cornell.edu, and ask in October whether it will sign for a capstone team rather than assuming it will. The agreement binds the university, and it binds you through the university.
Read the licence on data you already have, too. Most of what the library pays for, WRDS and Compustat included, is licensed for academic, non-commercial use. A project a firm would pay for cannot be built on a file whose licence forbids commercial use.
Two consequences worth planning around: you may not be able to show your results, and the agreement may not be signed in time. If your project depends on a DUA, it needs a plan B by meeting 5.

title: Permissions and ethics
text:
Where the file lives
Cornell classifies data as low, moderate or high risk. Anything under FERPA sits at moderate risk. Identifiers paired with a name, health records and financial account data sit at high risk. Proprietary and licensed data are covered by the same rule.
Nothing at moderate risk or above goes into a publicly available AI tool. That is Cornell’s rule, in its own words, and anything you put into a public tool is treated as public. The approved tools are listed on that page. If the file you hold is not one you may upload, the assistant sees the column names and five invented rows, and the code it writes runs on your laptop.
Removing the names is not de-identification. ZIP code, birth date and sex together identify most Americans uniquely. Coarsen what you do not need at full resolution, and collect only what the question needs.

Where to ask

The IRB office answers questions before submission, and would much rather hear from you early than fix a protocol later.
Ask me first if you are unsure whether any of this applies. Usually it does not take long to find out, and the answer changes what you can design.

title: Where to get data
text:
Through the Cornell library
All of these need only a netID.

Companies and finance

WRDS (Wharton Research Data Services) — the standard academic host for historical finance and accounting data. Extensive, with use restrictions; talk to a librarian before pulling anything large.
Capital IQ — 88,000 public and 825,000 private companies: financials, transactions, people.
Refinitiv Workspace — company financials, market data, transactions, analyst reports. Register with your Cornell email.
PitchBook — private equity and venture capital deals, investors, comparables. Log in with SSO using your Cornell address.
Mergent Intellect and Data Axle Reference Solutions — private company directories, US and international.
EDGAR — every SEC filing, free and public, no login at all.

Bloomberg terminals are physical machines: three at Mann Library on the main level, plus the Management, Hotel and Law libraries. Worth an hour even if your project never uses one.


Markets and industries
Mintel · Passport (Euromonitor) · Statista · IBISWorld (700+ US industries) · Frost & Sullivan · Technavio (20 downloads per Cornell email per month) · Business Source Complete · ABI/Inform.
These are reports, not microdata. They are excellent for sizing a market and for the background half of a feasibility memo. They will not give you anything to estimate on.


Demographics and geography
SimplyAnalytics builds thematic maps and reports from US demographic, business and marketing data — the fastest way to check whether a geographic question is even viable. Then the free federal sources: data.census.gov, BLS, and the Consumer Expenditure Survey.

title: Where to get data
text:
Restricted data, through CCSS
The Cornell Center for Social Sciences runs Cornell’s secure data services, and holds things you cannot get any other way.

Kilts-Nielsen marketing data — Consumer Panel, Retail Scanner (weekly price and volume from 90+ retail chains across all US markets), Ad Intel advertising data from 2010, and the PanelViews surveys. For Business of Food or Behavioral Marketing this is close to the best data in the world for the question.
Getting it is a project, not a download. The data lives in CCSS’s Regulated Research Environment, and access means applying through Cornell Research Services and requesting project space. Budget months, and start by emailing socialsciences@cornell.edu.






There is also a public-use extract in the CCSS archive, open to any Cornell netID. Be clear about what it is: retail sales of coffee, laundry detergent and shampoo, by US region, brand, size, packaging, UPC and price, for 2019 only. That is a dataset for practising on, not one to build a capstone on. Do not plan a project around it.



FSRDC — confidential Census, BLS and NCHS microdata, through one of 30 Federal Statistical Research Data Centers. Requires federal project approval and takes longer than this degree.
IAB@Cornell — German administrative labour-market microdata.

title: Where to get data
text:
Free and public, worth knowing

FRED — 800,000+ economic series, the fastest macro source there is.
IPUMS — harmonised census and survey microdata, US and international. Free with registration.
ICPSR — the largest social science data archive; Cornell is a member.
Roper Center — public opinion polling, hosted at Cornell.
World Bank Open Data and UN Comtrade — the backbone for International Development Economics, where Dewey is weakest.
Zillow research data and the Redfin Data Center — free housing indices at ZIP and metro level.
County assessor and deeds records — public in most US counties. Worth knowing that this is precisely what ATTOM, the source behind Dewey’s Real Estate Transaction Data, already packages nationally and cleans for you. Going to a county directly is worth it only for a specific reason: one county in unusual depth, a longer history than ATTOM carries, or a field it does not hold.

title: Where to get data
text:
Collecting it yourself
Sometimes nobody has your data. That usually means nobody has asked your question. It is a good sign, not a problem.

Surveys. Cornell provides Qualtrics to all students. Fielding to a paid sample through Prolific or MTurk costs real but small money and needs no programming.
Online experiments. A message test, a price test, or a conjoint task can be built in Qualtrics and fielded the same way.
Asking a firm. The most ambitious project anyone here remembers talked a soda company into donating thousands of cans for a field experiment. People say yes more often than students expect.

All of this needs IRB clearance — see permissions and ethics, and start it early.

title: Design scenarios — defence cards
text:
Eight settings. Cut along the dashed lines and deal one
per team. Cards 1–4 suit meeting 7 (experiments, instruments,
discontinuities); cards 5–8 suit meeting 8 (difference-in-differences, fixed
effects, event studies). Page 2 is the defence sheet.




  
    Card 1 · meeting 7
    The savings nudge
    A bank wants to know whether its monthly financial-literacy email
    makes customers save more. It has 400,000 customers on the list, it
    controls who receives what, and it can wait six months.
    Defend: what design, and what does it cost them to run it properly?
  

  
    Card 2 · meeting 7
    The scholarship cutoff
    A university awards a scholarship to every applicant scoring above
    1200 on an entrance test, and to nobody below. Administrators want to
    know whether the money raises graduation rates.
    Defend: what design — and who exactly does your estimate apply to?
  

  
    Card 3 · meeting 7
    The water filters
    An NGO distributed water filters to the villages that asked for
    them. Diarrhoea rates fell in those villages and not in others. The
    donor wants to know whether the filters worked.
    Defend: a design — or defend the claim that this cannot honestly be answered.
  

  
    Card 4 · meeting 7
    The local label
    A food company is deciding whether to put "locally sourced" on a
    package. It wants to know what that claim is worth in cents per unit
    before it commits to the supply chain.
    Defend: what design, and what is the gap between what it measures and what they want?
  

  
    Card 5 · meeting 8
    The self-checkout rollout
    A grocery chain installed self-checkout in 340 of its 900 stores
    over eighteen months, region by region, in an order set by an old
    refurbishment schedule. Did basket size change?
    Defend: what design — and what does "region by region" buy you?
  

  
    Card 6 · meeting 8
    The border wage
    One state raised its minimum wage on 1 January; the state across
    the river did not. There are fast-food restaurants within two miles
    of the border on both sides.
    Defend: what design, and what has to be true about the two sides?
  

  
    Card 7 · meeting 8
    The light rail
    A city opened a light-rail line four years ago. House prices within
    half a mile of the new stations are up 22% since. The transit
    authority would like to claim credit.
    Defend: what design — and why is the naive comparison almost certainly wrong?
  

  
    Card 8 · meeting 8
    The seller fee
    A platform raised its commission for seller accounts created on or
    after 1 March, leaving older accounts on the old rate. It wants to
    know whether the higher fee drove sellers away.
    Defend: what design, and what would make the two groups not comparable?

Where to read more

title: 11 · Figures
text:
Session A · 2:00–3:15
Three blocks. First, which figure answers which question. Distributions: a histogram, a density, a boxplot and a cumulative curve of the same column tell you four different things, and only some of them show you the second bump. Time: levels, indexed to a base year, or on a log scale — that choice is a claim about whether the reader should care about dollars or about growth rates. Space: a map of counts is a map of population unless you divided by something. Comparison: a sorted dot plot beats a bar chart nearly every time, and error bars are part of the estimate rather than decoration. Underneath all of it is one instinct — look at the data before you model it. Anscombe’s quartet makes the case in one slide. Four datasets, the same means, the same variances, the same correlation, the same fitted line. One is a clean relationship, one is a curve, one is a line with a single outlier dragging it, one is a vertical stack where one point does all the work. The regression output is identical for all four. Second block: what figures hide. Aggregation, and the Berkeley graduate admissions case of 1973, where the university looked like it admitted women at a much lower rate overall while most departments taken one at a time did not. Scale, and axes that start where the author wanted them to. Binning, where the width of a histogram bin decides whether there is one group in your data or two. Projection, and Greenland the size of Africa. Area scaled by radius, which doubles the number and quadruples the ink. Cherry-picked windows. Counts where you needed a rate. Then the move that makes those useful: read a published figure for what it is not showing. Where is the denominator. What happened before the window starts. What do the subgroups do. What happened to the units that dropped out of the sample partway through. Third block, and it is the hard one. An honest figure that still makes a point. Honest does not mean neutral. You choose the comparison, sort the categories, show the raw points behind the summary, split one aggregate into small multiples, annotate the single number the argument turns on, and write the claim in the title instead of a label. Zeroing the axis is not a rule — for an index, a growth rate or a difference, zero is the wrong anchor. The test is whether the axis matches the quantity. And a finished figure has a sentence. If you cannot write the sentence, the figure is not finished.

title: 11 · Figures
text:
Session B · 3:30–4:30
Every session B opens with a ten-minute team check-in: what you did since last week, what is stuck, and who is doing what next. Written down, and handed in with that session’s work.
Six figures, each lying a different way, one per team, twenty minutes. A truncated axis turning three points of satisfaction into a soaring bar chart. Two axes on unrelated scales manufacturing a correlation between ad spend and sales. Four quarters shown out of eight years. An aggregate rising while every single region falls. Circles where two million got twice the radius of one million, so the picture is four times bigger and not two. Complaints by state with no population underneath. Name the trick, say what the figure is entitled to claim, and redraw it honestly on the sheet. The redraw still has to make a point, and that is where most teams stall — naming the lie takes two minutes, replacing it takes the rest. Then one team is drawn at random to put its redraw at the front while the room attacks, and we draw again as far as the clock allows. Points for an attack that lands, and you have to name the trick rather than say you dislike the picture. Card 4 is the aggregation one and card 6 is the rate one. Those two are where the morning either landed or it did not. Then your own project, on paper, by hand. Draw the one figure it lives or dies on. Not a figure — the figure, the one a reader looks at before deciding whether to believe you. For most of you it is one of three: the picture showing that your variation exists, the picture showing your comparison group looked like your treated group before anything happened, or the picture showing the outcome move. You do not have the data yet, so you draw it empty. Both axes labelled with their units. What one point on it is. Which comparison is on the page. The claim written across the top as a sentence. Then draw it a second time as it would look if you are wrong. If the two drawings look the same, the figure cannot support the claim, and finding that out in November is cheap. Both drawings are handed in before you leave.
Your team’s output is submitted before you leave.
